CCBS Lecture 13 · Demonstrations · 19 October 2026

Begin with Part 2: describing behavior through objectives and biochemical constraints. Then use its steady flux calculations. Continue to its dynamic constraints. The exposition derives the equations. Every control works offline. The organism and control trajectories are precomputed solutions of the declared problems. Their controls select or replay those solutions.

Optional comparison: a static function, a trajectory and a controller from optimization

The core’s spring-carriage experiment compares an explicit force law with an optimization at each stage. Change the load, follow the motion, then request faster feedback under a motor limit. It belongs to the optional machine-design extension outside the five metabolic experiments.

Experiment 1 of 5

1Allocate a limited ATP supply

Ask the room: which flux allocations satisfy the same balance, and which one gives maximum growth?

The intermediate balance imposes v1=v2v_1=v_2. ATP balance imposes v1=w+vgrowv_1=w+v_{\mathrm{grow}}. The input flux satisfies 0≤v1≤U0\leq v_1\leq U. The growth outlet consumes ATP and no retained intermediate. All fluxes use one shared illustrative unit.

Investment v1v_1Payoff v2v_2Growth vgrowv_{\mathrm{grow}}Free coefficient α\alpha
Show the matrix calculation and the free coefficient

The two steady balances determine a line of flux vectors. For the investment coefficient one, write

S=(1−10−12−1),Sv=(0w),S†=(11/301/3−1−2/3).S=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad Sv=\begin{pmatrix}0\\w\end{pmatrix},\qquad S^{\dagger}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1/3\\0&1/3\\-1&-2/3\end{pmatrix}.

The pseudoinverse supplies one particular solution. Adding any multiple of (1,1,1)T(1,1,1)^{\mathsf T} leaves both balances unchanged:

v=w3(11−2)+α(111)=(w+vgroww+vgrowvgrow),α=2w3+vgrow.v=\frac w3\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\alpha\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}w+v_{\mathrm{grow}}\\w+v_{\mathrm{grow}}\\v_{\mathrm{grow}}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\alpha=\frac{2w}{3}+v_{\mathrm{grow}}.

Nonnegative growth and the input cap restrict the coefficient. The slider moves across that interval:

2w3≤α≤U−w3,0≤vgrow≤U−w.\frac{2w}{3}\leq\alpha\leq U-\frac w3,\qquad0\leq v_{\mathrm{grow}}\leq U-w.

Maximum growth is U−wU-w when U≥wU\geq w. When U<wU<w, the interval is empty. Calling that optimum zero would hide the failed maintenance balance. The core first solves the two-reaction matrix by inversion, then derives this pseudoinverse family.

A maximum is a bound under specified constraints. Infeasibility means the stated steady requirements cannot all be met.

2Change nutrient constraints in an E. coli reconstruction

Ask the room: does increasing oxygen always increase the maximum growth rate?

The iJO1366 model has 1,805 compartment-specific metabolite rows and 2,583 reactions in this archived file. It maximizes its core biomass reaction. ATP maintenance has a lower bound of 3.15 mmol per gram dry weight per hour. Uptake caps use the same flux unit. The biomass normalization gives growth in inverse hours.1

Inspect all 2,583 reactions and download the table

This table compares oxygen caps 0, 5 and 20 at a fixed glucose cap of 10. It does not follow the glucose selector above. Bounds are the archived model bounds before these scenario changes. Negative exchange flux denotes uptake.

Reaction and signed stoichiometryModel boundsOxygen 0Oxygen 5Oxygen 20

Nutrient constraints change the best achievable steady objective. They do not specify an ATP concentration or its recovery trajectory.

3Compare binding-derived reaction orders with stability

Ask the room: can a productive ATP-binding site stabilize this ATP-investment pathway by itself?

Hold baseline pools and fluxes fixed at (qˉI,qˉATP)=(1/1.1,1)(\bar q_I,\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}})=(1/1.1,1) and vˉ1=vˉ2=wˉ=1\bar v_1=\bar v_2=\bar w=1. Let aa be the upstream ATP reaction order. Hold downstream ATP reaction order b=−0.3b=-0.3 and downstream intermediate reaction order one. The general slider changes the local slope while matching the operating point. It does not specify a complete binding mechanism.

Compare with an explicit productive binding law

For trace enzyme, rapid equilibrium and fixed total enzyme, v=VqATP/(Kd+qATP)v=Vq_{\mathrm{ATP}}/(K_d+q_{\mathrm{ATP}}) gives a=Kd/(Kd+qATP)a=K_d/(K_d+q_{\mathrm{ATP}}). Free ATP is approximated by total ATP under the trace-enzyme assumption. Changing ATP occupancy below selects a binding-derived slope. The comparison rescales capacity to retain the same reference flux.

Every such productive-site slope is positive. None enters the stable interval. ATP inhibition can supply negative slopes, but excessive inhibition crosses the other stability boundary.

A=(−1.1a+0.32.2−a−0.6),−1.7<a<0.A=\begin{pmatrix}-1.1&a+0.3\\2.2&-a-0.6\end{pmatrix},\qquad -1.7<a<0.

For an animated comparison of ATP autocatalysis and a motor-controlled inverted pendulum, open the optional experiment in core Section 3. It shows how increasing the restoring feedback also reduces damping in this architecture.

Optional · Compare steady compensation, resonance and conserved robustness

Use the same inhibition gains to compare steady regulation and transient cost. Here h=1−ah=1-a, so the marked gains h=1.2,2.0,2.4,2.6h=1.2,2.0,2.4,2.6 correspond to reaction orders a=−0.2,−1.0,−1.4,−1.6a=-0.2,-1.0,-1.4,-1.6. Baseline pools, fluxes, κ=1.1\kappa=1.1 and g=0.3g=0.3 remain fixed. The local steady ATP error-to-demand ratio is 1/(h−1)1/(h-1), while stability requires 1<h<2.71<h<2.7.

The sensitivity plots show how feedback redistributes disturbance rejection across frequency. The dimensionless feedback sensitivity is Sh(s)=(s2+2.7s−1.1)/[s2+(2.7−h)s+1.1(h−1)]\mathcal S_h(s)=(s^2+2.7s-1.1)/[s^2+(2.7-h)s+1.1(h-1)]. Here ss is the Laplace variable, evaluated at s=iωs=i\omega for angular frequency ω\omega in the normalized clock. This sensitivity is the feedback factor, not the ATP response amplitude. The final plot uses r=(2/π)arctan⁡(ω/1.1)r=(2/\pi)\arctan(\omega/1.1), which includes the frequency weighting. Its positive area minus negative area is 0.6786 for every stable gain. The transformed coordinate includes all frequencies, with infinite frequency at the right endpoint.

Choose a gain or move the slider. The baseline stays fixed. All responses are local to that baseline. Scroll each plot sideways on a narrow screen.

The same four colors mark the same gains in every plot. Rings mark the selected gain. The slider stays inside the stable interval.

Identical balanced fluxes can have different local stability. Binding information restricts the reaction orders that can supply that stability.

4Replay an optimized glycolytic transient

Ask the room: what does changing the cost of enzyme activity adjustments do to the ATP response?

This replay reproduces the executable 2023 flux exponent control example. It uses vˉ1=2qˉATPu1\bar v_1=2\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}u_1 and vˉ2=2.2qˉIu2\bar v_2=2.2\bar q_Iu_2. The controller penalizes pool deviations and changes in log activity over a finite prediction horizon. At time zero, demand rises from 1 to 1.1 and the reference pools also change. This is not a demand-only adaptation experiment.2

Show the assumptions behind the replay

The state cost is Q=diag⁡(0.3,0.08)Q=\operatorname{diag}(0.3,0.08). The initial activities are e−0.695e^{-0.695}. The target changes from (1/1.1,1)(1/1.1,1) to (1/1.1+0.07,0.93)(1/1.1+0.07,0.93). These settings follow the executable notebook. The printed paper caption uses a different target. Predicted pool floors are inactive. This example imposes neither an enzyme activity ceiling nor an explicit binding reaction-order polytope. The exposition separates the flux exponent control framework from this illustrative controller.

An optimized trajectory follows from a plant, admissible controls and a cost. A successful fit alone does not identify a molecular regulator.

5Trade growth allocation for ATP protection

Ask the room: if growth pauses, must that improve total growth over the next ten time units?

Both policies control the same nonlinear plant: vˉ1=qˉATP−2u1\bar v_1=\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}^{-2}u_1, vˉ2=2qˉIu2\bar v_2=2\bar q_Iu_2 and vˉgrow=qˉATPugrow\bar v_{\mathrm{grow}}=\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}u_{\mathrm{grow}}. Demand increases from 0.6 to 1.4 at time zero. One policy can pause growth. The other keeps growth activity at least 0.05. Both reward growth allocation and an ATP reserve. These new calculations use the source slides’ reaction structure.

Show the optimization problem

At each step, minimize ∑k=019{0.1[−vˉgrow,k+10(qˉATP,k−1)2]+0.02∥uk−uk−1∥2}\sum_{k=0}^{19}\{0.1[-\bar v_{\mathrm{grow},k}+10(\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP},k}-1)^2]+0.02\|u_k-u_{k-1}\|^2\} along the nonlinear plant. Require 10−4≤u1,u2≤110^{-4}\leq u_1,u_2\leq1, 0≤ugrow≤10\leq u_{\mathrm{grow}}\leq1 and pool floors qˉI≥0.05,qˉATP≥0.5\bar q_I\geq0.05,\bar q_{\mathrm{ATP}}\geq0.5. The second policy changes only the growth activity floor to 0.05. The horizon is two normalized time units. Only the first control is applied before replanning. These are local numerical optima. The exposition provides the full interpretation.

Pausing growth protects ATP and lowers the stated combined cost here. It reduces integrated growth allocation over the comparison interval.
